about.title: Slope-Intercept Form and Graphing Lines
about.length_note: About 30 minutes. There are 16 short steps, one idea each, and a quick check after most of them. That is enough time to learn the form, graph it step by step, and read what m and b mean, without rushing. Anyone who wants more time can pause after any step and replay it.

sources.title: 4.5 Use the Slope–Intercept Form of an Equation of a Line (Elementary Algebra)
Graphing a Line Using the Slope and Y-Intercept

say.text: Today you'll learn to draw a line straight from its equation, and to say what its numbers mean in real life.

show.text: Graph a line from y = mx + b

say.text: First, a quick reminder from last class. Slope tells how steep a line is. It is rise over run: the change in y over the change in x.

ask.q: A line goes up 3 and right 2 on each step. What is its slope?
ask.why: The rise is 3 and the run is 2, so slope = rise ÷ run = 3/2.

say.text: Next idea: the y-intercept. It is the point where the line crosses the y-axis. On that axis x is 0, so the point looks like (0, b).

show.text: A coordinate grid. A line crosses the vertical y-axis at one marked dot, labeled (0, b).

ask.q: A line crosses the y-axis at 5. What is its y-intercept point?
ask.why: On the y-axis x is 0, so the point is (0, 5). The number you cross at goes second.

say.text: Now we put slope and y-intercept into one equation: y = mx + b. The m is the slope. The b is the y-intercept. Some books call it the y-form.
You have seen this before. In 8th grade, the standard says a line crossing the vertical axis at b has this equation.

show.text: y = mx + b for a line intercepting the vertical axis at b

say.text: To read m and b, look at the equation. In y = 2x + 3, the number with x is m, so m = 2. The number on its own is b, so b = 3.
Two tricky cases. If x has no number, as in y = −x + 4, then m = −1. And a minus sign belongs to the number after it, so in y = 4x − 5, b = −5.

ask.q: In y = 4x − 5, what are m and b?
ask.why: The number with x is the slope, 4. The number on its own is −5, because the minus sign goes with the 5.

say.text: Now we graph. Take y = 2x + 1. Step one: plot the y-intercept. Here b = 1, so put a dot at (0, 1).

show.text: A coordinate grid with one dot on the y-axis at (0, 1).

ask.q: To graph y = 3x − 2, which point do you plot first?
ask.why: Step one always uses b. Here b = −2, so the first point is (0, −2).

say.text: Step two: use the slope. Here m = 2, which is 2/1. From your dot, go up 2 and right 1. A positive slope climbs as you move right.

show.text: The same grid. An arrow goes from (0, 1) up 2 and right 1 to a second dot at (1, 3).

ask.q: You are at (0, 1) and the slope is 2. Which point comes next?
ask.why: Slope 2 = 2/1. Go up 2 and right 1: (0, 1) becomes (1, 3).

say.text: Step three: connect the two dots with a straight line. Add arrows at both ends, because the line keeps going.

show.text: A straight line through (0, 1) and (1, 3), with arrowheads at both ends.

say.text: Now a negative slope. For y = −x + 4, start at (0, 4). The slope −1 is −1/1, so go down 1 and right 1. A negative slope falls as you move right.

show.text: A grid. A dot at (0, 4), an arrow down 1 and right 1, and a second dot at (1, 3). A line slopes downward through them.

ask.q: For y = −x + 4, you start at (0, 4). Which point comes next?
ask.why: The slope is −1/1: down 1, right 1. So (0, 4) becomes (1, 3).

say.text: Now the meaning. In a real situation, b is the starting value, when x is 0. And m is the rate of change, how much y changes for each 1 of x.

show.text: b = starting value (x = 0) | m = change in y for each 1 step in x

say.text: Example: Sam has $20 saved and adds $5 every week. With x as weeks and y as dollars, that is y = 5x + 20. Here b = 20 and m = 5.

ask.q: In y = 5x + 20, what does the 20 mean?
ask.right: Sam starts with $20 before any weeks pass.
ask.why: b is the value when x = 0, which is the start. The 5 is the weekly change.

say.text: Let's use it. Put x = 3 weeks into y = 5x + 20. That is 5 times 3, plus 20. Look at the chart to check.

ask.q: Using y = 5x + 20, how many dollars does Sam have after 3 weeks?
ask.why: 5 × 3 = 15 dollars saved, plus the $20 he began with, makes $35.

say.text: A slope can be negative, too. Pretend a game's battery starts at 100 percent and drains a steady 10 points an hour: y = −10x + 100.

ask.q: In y = −10x + 100, what does the −10 mean?
ask.right: The battery drops 10 points each hour.
wrong: The battery takes 10 hours to charge.
ask.why: The slope is the rate of change. A negative slope means y goes down, here 10 points per hour. The 100 is the starting charge.

say.text: One last idea. If b is 0, the line goes through (0, 0), and we call it proportional. If b is not 0, it is still a straight line, but not proportional.

show.text: y = mx (b = 0): through (0, 0), proportional | y = mx + b (b ≠ 0): not through (0, 0), not proportional

ask.q: Arcade A costs $2 a game: y = 2x. Arcade B has a $5 entry plus $2 a game: y = 2x + 5. Which is proportional?
ask.right: Arcade A, because b = 0 and its line goes through (0, 0).
wrong: Arcade B, because it has a $5 entry.
Neither, because both are straight lines.
ask.why: Only y = 2x has b = 0. Both are linear with slope 2, but only Arcade A is proportional.

say.text: Recap. Read m and b. Plot (0, b). Use m as rise over run. Connect the dots. In a story, b is the start and m is the change.

show.text: 1. Read m and b | 2. Plot (0, b) | 3. Use rise ÷ run for the next point | 4. Connect with a line | Story: b = start, m = change per step

ask.q: What is the best first step to graph y = −2x + 6?
wrong: Draw a line, then look for the dots.
ask.why: Start with b = 6, the y-intercept, so plot (0, 6). Then use the slope −2 to find the next point.

notes.topic: Other ways to write a line

other_side.claim: In Algebra 1, any equation y = mx + b counts as a linear function.
other_side.other_view: Not everyone uses the word this way. Some advanced math texts use "linear function" only for lines through the origin (b = 0). Algebra 1 and 8th-grade standards use the wider meaning, so a line with b ≠ 0 still counts here.

other_side.claim: A line like y = 5x + 20 or y = −10x + 100 describes real life.
other_side.other_view: It only does if the rate of change really stays steady. Real savings, and real batteries, often speed up or slow down. So a line is a model that works while the rate stays roughly constant. It is not a perfect copy of reality.
